A client portal is worth building when your team answers the same three questions every day: "where is my report?", "what is the status?" and "can you resend the invoice?". The portal is a login-protected area on your own website where each client company sees its own documents, job status, invoices and support requests, and nobody else's. For a service business choosing a web development company in Pune to build one, the hard part is not the screens. It is the access rules that keep one client's files away from another, a login method your clients will actually use, private file storage, and a feed from the systems where your team already works. A first version usually takes six to twelve weeks; the rest can follow in phases.

This guide is for owners and operations heads of consultancies, agencies, engineering service firms, training providers and facility-services companies. It covers when a portal beats shared folders and WhatsApp, the six modules, data isolation, login, document storage, notifications, integration, three build routes with indicative costs and a phased rollout.

## When a portal is worth building, and when it is not

A shared Drive folder per client and a WhatsApp group work well for longer than most software vendors admit.

**Shared folders and WhatsApp are enough when:**

- you have fewer than about fifteen to twenty active clients, each with one contact person;
- documents are not sensitive, and nobody needs proof of who downloaded what;
- status questions are occasional, not daily.

**A portal starts paying for itself when:**

- several people at each client need access, and they change jobs;
- the same document is requested repeatedly: test certificates, attendance sheets, monthly reports, invoice copies;
- your staff spend a measurable part of each day answering status questions (count them for two weeks before commissioning anything);
- clients' procurement or audit teams ask how you control access to their data;
- work runs to a pattern (jobs, batches, site visits, monthly cycles), so status can be shown without someone typing an update.

One honest test: if your internal records are themselves in WhatsApp and individual spreadsheets, fix that first, or the portal will show clients an empty page.

## The six modules of a service-business portal

Most service portals are built from the same six parts.

### 1. Client company, users and profile

The basic unit is the client company, not the individual. Each company has one or more users, a primary contact, addresses and the name of your account manager. Let the client's own administrator invite and remove colleagues, so that access changes do not wait for your team.

### 2. Documents

Two directions: files you publish to the client (reports, certificates, drawings, contracts) and files the client uploads (purchase orders, inputs, signed forms). Each document needs a type, the job or period it belongs to, a version and an upload date.

### 3. Project or job status

A list of active jobs, each with a stage from a fixed list, the next milestone, the date and who is responsible. Keep stages few and plain: "Scheduled, In progress, Awaiting your input, Under review, Delivered". "Awaiting your input" matters most: it tells the client the delay is on their side without anyone having to say so.

### 4. Invoices and statements to view

A read-only list of invoices with number, date, amount, due date and status, each with a PDF download, plus an account statement. This is a view of what your accounting system already holds. It removes the "please resend the invoice" email. Payment collection is a separate decision and outside the scope of this article.

### 5. Tickets and requests

A form to raise a request with a category, the related job, a description and attachments; a reference number; a visible status; and a thread of replies. A request then has an owner and a history, which a WhatsApp message does not.

### 6. Announcements

Short notices from you, targeted by client group: holiday schedules, a changed contact person, planned maintenance. It is the cheapest module to build.

## Roles and keeping each client's data separate

This is where portals fail, and it is where to spend review time. OWASP's Top 10 for 2025 ranks broken access control first among web application risks, and lists "permitting viewing or editing someone else's account by providing its unique identifier" among the common weaknesses. In plain terms: a user logged in as Client A changes `invoice/1041` to `invoice/1042` in the address bar and sees Client B's invoice. The page was login-protected; it never checked whose invoice it was.

### The rules to insist on

OWASP's prevention guidance translates into a short list you can put in the contract:

- **Deny by default.** Every page and every file is private unless it is deliberately public.
- **Check ownership on the server for every request.** Each record carries a client-company ID, and every query filters by the logged-in user's company. Hiding a menu item in the browser is not access control.
- **Write the check once and reuse it** across every screen.
- **Test it.** Ask for automated tests that log in as Client A and try to fetch Client B's records, run before each release.
- **Log access-control failures**, alert an administrator when they repeat, and rate-limit the endpoints so a script cannot walk through ID numbers.

Long random identifiers in URLs are a sensible extra layer, not a substitute for the ownership check.

### A workable role set

On the client side, three roles cover most needs: a user who sees the company's jobs, documents and tickets; a finance user who also sees invoices and statements; and an administrator who can invite and remove colleagues. On your side, staff see only the clients assigned to them, the accounts team sees invoices across clients, and one administrator manages roles, settings and the audit log.

## Login: password with MFA, OTP or passkeys

Choose by who your clients' users are and how sensitive the documents are. Passwords with a second factor suit office users, at the price of reset requests. One-time codes suit occasional users. Passkeys suit regular users on recent devices and need a fallback.

### If you use passwords

NIST's SP 800-63B, in its current fourth revision, and OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet agree on rules that contradict older habits:

- Minimum length of 15 characters where the password is the only factor, and 8 where it is combined with a second factor.
- Accept passphrases of at least 64 characters, and allow paste and password managers.
- Do not force a mix of capitals, digits and symbols, or periodic changes. Require a change only on evidence of compromise.
- Check new passwords against a blocklist of common and breached passwords.
- Give the same message whether or not the email exists, and throttle failed attempts per account.

For resets, OWASP's Forgot Password Cheat Sheet adds: a random single-use token that expires, no automatic login after the reset, and an email telling the user the password was changed.

### If you use one-time codes

OTP login is popular because nobody has to remember anything. Know its limits. NIST states that authenticators requiring a code to be typed in "shall not be considered phishing-resistant", restricts the use of the telephone network (SMS and voice) for delivering codes, and says email shall not be used for out-of-band authentication. NIST writes for US federal systems and does not bind a Pune business, but it states fairly where the risk lies. For routine reports, an emailed or SMS code is a reasonable choice. For contracts, personal data or anything regulated, add a second factor or offer passkeys. Our article on [mobile-number OTP login](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-otp-login-sms-whatsapp-dlt-2026) covers delivery channels, abuse limits and fallbacks for online stores; the build is the same.

### Passkeys

A passkey replaces the password with a key pair. Your server stores only the public key, and the user confirms with the device's screen lock. Google's web.dev guidance explains that the signature is issued only on the valid domain, which makes passkeys resistant to phishing. A practical pattern: verify the user by email the first time, offer a passkey after login, and keep a recovery route. See [why passkeys are replacing passwords](/blog/web-development-company-pune-passkeys-authentication-2026) for the detail.

### Sessions

OWASP's Session Management Cheat Sheet asks for session cookies marked `Secure` and `HttpOnly` with `SameSite` set, a new session ID after login, server-side invalidation on logout, and both an idle and an absolute timeout. It suggests idle timeouts of 15 to 30 minutes for low-risk applications and much shorter for high-value ones.

## Document storage: private files, signed links, scanning and retention

- **Private storage.** Files go into a storage bucket or a directory outside the public web folder, never a media library where anyone with the link can open them. OWASP's File Upload Cheat Sheet recommends a separate host or, failing that, storage outside the webroot.
- **Short-lived signed links.** When a user clicks download, the application checks that the user may see that file and then issues a link valid for a few minutes.
- **Uploads from clients.** Allow only the file types you need, check the real file type and not just the extension or the browser's stated type, rename files to random names on the server, set a size limit and require login to upload.
- **Malware scanning.** Scan uploads before your staff can open them, and keep unscanned files in quarantine.
- **Download log.** Record who downloaded what and when.
- **Retention.** Decide per document type how long files stay after a contract ends, and automate deletion or archiving.

## Notifications by email and WhatsApp

Send a message when something changes that the client cares about: a document published, a job stage changed, input needed from them, a ticket answered, an invoice issued.

- **Email** is the default for business users. Send from your own domain and link to the item.
- **WhatsApp** suits field contacts and owners who live on their phones. Business-initiated messages go through the WhatsApp Business Platform using pre-approved templates. Meta defines a utility template as non-promotional and specific to, or requested by, the user, which fits "Your report for job 2417 is ready". Record each user's opt-in, and see our [WhatsApp Business API](/whatsapp/business-api) page for how the set-up works.
- **Keep content out of the message.** "A new document is available. Log in to view" is the pattern. Never attach an invoice or a report to a notification.

## Connecting the portal to your CRM and accounting system

If staff have to type status into the portal after typing it somewhere else, the portal will be out of date within a month. Feed it from the systems of record.

- **Client and contact list** from the CRM, one direction to begin with.
- **Job status** from wherever jobs are managed: a CRM, a project tool or an operations system.
- **Invoices** from the accounting system: the invoice record and its PDF, read-only.
- **Tickets** live in the portal and are pushed to the CRM, or live in a helpdesk tool and are displayed in the portal.

There are two ways to connect:

1. **By API**, where the source system offers one. Changes appear in near real time.
2. **By scheduled export**, where it does not. The source system writes a file (CSV or similar) at a set interval and the portal imports it. For invoices a nightly update is normally acceptable.

Either way, decide which system owns each field, give every record a stable ID shared by both sides, log each sync run and alert someone when one fails. Show a "last updated" time on invoice and status screens. If you do not yet have a CRM that holds jobs and client contacts in one place, that is the first project; our [CRM development](/services/ci-crm) page describes what we build.

## Three build routes a web development company in Pune can offer

| | WordPress with membership and portal plugins | Off-the-shelf SaaS portal | Custom build |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best for | Up to a few dozen clients, documents and announcements, simple status | Standard needs, fast start, no in-house IT | Several roles, integrations, your own workflow |
| Per-client data isolation | Depends on the plugin and on careful configuration; needs testing | Built in | Designed and tested for your rules |
| Integration | Limited; often by import | What the vendor's connectors offer | Whatever your systems allow |
| Indicative set-up cost | ₹60,000 to ₹2,00,000 | Little or none | ₹3,00,000 to ₹12,00,000 or more |
| Indicative running cost | ₹30,000 to ₹90,000 a year (hosting, licences, updates) | Per-user or per-client subscription, often quoted in US dollars; confirm current pricing with the vendor | ₹60,000 to ₹2,50,000 a year (hosting, monitoring, support) |
| Typical timeline | 4 to 8 weeks | 1 to 3 weeks to configure | 10 to 20 weeks for a first release |
| Main risk | Plugin conflicts; private files left in a public media folder | Recurring cost grows with users; your data sits in the vendor's format | Higher first cost; depends on a clear specification |

All rupee figures are indicative ranges for planning, not quotations. They vary with the number of modules, roles, integrations and languages.

**Normally included in a build price:** screen design, the agreed modules, access rules with tests, one login method with recovery, private file storage, email notifications, an admin panel, deployment and a short support period.

**Normally quoted separately:** each third-party integration, WhatsApp set-up and message charges, migration of old documents, an independent security test, native mobile apps and changes after sign-off.

On the SaaS route, ask two questions before signing: can you export all documents and records in a usable format if you leave, and where is the data hosted. On the WordPress route, ask to be shown, logged out, that a document URL does not open.

## A phased rollout plan

**Phase 0, two to three weeks: prepare.** Count requests, list document types, agree job stages, clean the contact list and choose five pilot clients.

**Phase 1, six to ten weeks: login, companies and users, documents, announcements.** Publish new documents only through the portal for pilot clients. Measure logins and the "please send" requests that remain.

**Phase 2, four to six weeks: job status and tickets.** Connect status to the system where jobs are managed. Keep a named person watching the ticket queue.

**Phase 3, three to five weeks: invoices and statements.** Read-only feed from accounting, with the finance-user role.

**Phase 4, ongoing: WhatsApp notifications, passkeys, reports, more clients.** Add clients in batches, each with a short walkthrough call.

During the rollout, keep answering on WhatsApp, but with a link to the portal item.

## Privacy, logs and what Indian rules expect

A client portal stores personal data: names, work emails, mobile numbers and login records of your clients' staff, and sometimes more inside the documents. Two points to raise with your developer and your adviser.

- **DPDP.** The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 with a phased start. According to published summaries of the notification, the rules on notice, security safeguards, breach intimation and retention take effect eighteen months after publication, which falls around mid-May 2027. Confirm the current position before you rely on that date. The safeguards described include encryption, access controls, logging and backups. Our article on [DPDP and website compliance](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026) explains the notice and consent side.
- **Logs.** CERT-In's directions of 28 April 2022 require service providers, intermediaries, data centres, bodies corporate and government organisations to enable logs of their ICT systems and maintain them securely for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, and to report specified cyber incidents within six hours of noticing them. Ask how login and download logs are kept and for how long, and take advice on how the directions apply to you.

This section describes what the rules say; it is not legal advice.

## A worked example

This is an illustration, not a client case.

An engineering inspection and testing firm in Pimpri-Chinchwad serves about 80 industrial clients, each with two to five contacts. Three coordinators spend much of each day resending test certificates.

- **Route chosen:** a custom build, because certificates must be tied to jobs and job data already sits in the firm's CRM.
- **Phase 1 (eight weeks):** client companies and users, a documents module where certificates are published per job, and announcements. Ten pilot clients. Login by email one-time code, with passkeys offered after first login.
- **Phase 2 (five weeks):** job status pulled from the CRM by API in five stages, and a ticket form with the category "re-test request".
- **Phase 3 (four weeks):** invoices imported nightly from the accounting system as records with PDFs, visible only to users with the finance role.
- **Indicative budget:** in the region of ₹6,00,000 to ₹8,00,000 across the three phases, plus running costs, on the ranges given above.

The firm does the same amount of work. What changes is that clients find certificates without a phone call, and the coordinators schedule visits instead of forwarding PDFs.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Treating login as access control.** Being logged in proves who the user is, not what they may see. Test cross-client access explicitly.
- **Putting private documents in a public folder** and relying on nobody guessing the link.
- **One shared login per client company.** You lose the audit trail, and the password leaves with each employee.
- **No owner.** Someone on your side must add clients, watch tickets and read failed-sync alerts.
- **Forgetting the exit.** Removing a client company and archiving its documents should be a designed function.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a client portal on a website?

A client portal is a login-protected section of a company's website where each customer sees only their own information, such as documents, project or job status, invoices and support requests. It replaces repeated emails and WhatsApp messages asking for files.

### How much does it cost to build a client portal in India?

As an indicative range, a WordPress-based portal with documents, announcements and simple status costs about ₹60,000 to ₹2,00,000 to set up, and a custom portal with roles, integrations and ticketing costs about ₹3,00,000 to ₹12,00,000 or more. Off-the-shelf SaaS portals have little set-up cost but charge a recurring subscription. Annual hosting and support are extra.

### How long does it take to build a customer portal?

A first phase with login, client users, documents and announcements typically takes six to ten weeks for a custom build, and four to eight weeks on WordPress. Job status, tickets and invoice views are usually added in later phases of three to six weeks each. Configuring a SaaS portal can take one to three weeks.

### Is OTP login secure enough for a client portal?

For a portal holding routine reports and status, a one-time code sent by email or SMS is a reasonable and convenient choice. Codes can be phished and depend on message delivery, so for sensitive documents add a second factor or offer passkeys. Whatever the method, limit login attempts and expire idle sessions.

### Can a client portal show invoices from Tally or other accounting software?

Yes. The portal can display invoice records and PDFs taken from your accounting system, either through an API where the software provides one or through a scheduled export and import. The portal shows a read-only copy with a "last updated" time, and your accounting system remains the record that counts.
